name: Olga Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm lead carpenter for a non-profit housing builder, the kind that puts up affordable rental homes for a housing co-op. We do timber-frame terraces, two storeys, about twenty homes on the current site out past the ring road. I start at seven with a coffee from the flask and a look at the day's walls, then I'm setting out, checking the framers' work and fixing stair openings that never quite match the drawings. I love standing in a finished frame before the boards go on, when you can see the whole house like a skeleton; what wears me out is chasing late deliveries of studs.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's it like being the lead on that crew?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mostly good now. When I started at nineteen there were blokes who'd ask to speak to "the carpenter" while I was holding the nail gun. These days the crew are fine, and two of my apprentices are women, which I'm proud of. I use one of those AI chat apps now and then to double-check a cut list or tidy up an email to the office, but I always check it against my own numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. We call it AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I half-say already: that it was useful for some paperwork but it was never going to frame a house. I'd probably post something sarcastic in the crew group chat, like a photo of a wonky stud with "the robots won't fix this one". People would laugh and move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means things stay as they are, which is pretty good. We've got years of work lined up because there's a housing shortage, and that doesn't go away because some software turned out to be oversold. Jonas and I could keep plodding towards our own place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and keep using the chat app for the boring bits. I'd go ahead with the setting-out course my boss has offered, the one for using a total station, which is a laser tool for marking out a site. And I'd keep putting about a fifth of my pay into savings like now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit smug maybe. Nice when the shouting turns out to be just shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change at the co-op office in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably they'd do the tenant forms and rota faster, which would honestly be good. The office is two people and they're drowning. If AI gives Priya back an afternoon a week, nobody's job goes and things get built faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd regret if this one happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe that I wasted some nights worrying. I read a lot of those scary articles at three in the morning last spring. I'd want those hours back.

S0.say: I'd say it was handy for paperwork but was never going to frame a house, and I'd post a joke photo of a wonky stud in the crew chat. People would laugh and move on.
S0.think: Privately it means things stay pretty good: there's a housing shortage and years of work lined up. Jonas and I keep plodding towards our own place.
S0.do: Keeps working and using the chat app for small admin tasks, and takes the total station setting-out course her boss offered. Keeps saving about a fifth of her pay.
S0.feel: Calm and a little smug, with a twinge of regret for the nights she lost reading scary articles.
S0.quote: I read a lot of those scary articles at three in the morning last spring. I'd want those hours back.
S0.fieldNote: Comfortable and secure in her trade, helped by a long housing pipeline. She already uses AI lightly and checks it, which fits her steady profile. The only cost she names is lost sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where we need good rules, so the change helps workers instead of just profits. I'd back the union pushing for training on paid time and for robots to be used for the heavy, dangerous stuff first. I'd say that in the pub and I'd probably sign a petition or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm all right. Carpentry on a site like ours is a hundred small decisions about wonky timber, and I'm the one who makes them. If a machine can cut panels in a factory, fine, someone still has to stand them up straight on a muddy plot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until a couple of the bigger firms had tried the new tools, see which ones actually work, and then ask my boss to send me on that training. I'd probably start using the AI app more, maybe for planning the week's sequence. Money-wise I'd keep saving the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. A bit curious, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The guys in the prefab factory down the road, maybe. Their work is the most repeatable, cutting and nailing the same panel all day. My cousin Bruno works there and he's already a bit jumpy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for others to go first. Why not jump in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen too many shiny gadgets come onto site and end up in the back of the van. We had a moisture-reading app that was wrong half the time. I'll pick it up once I've seen it work on someone else's job.

S1.say: I'd say we need good rules so change helps workers and not just profits: paid training and robots on the heavy, dangerous work first. I'd say it in the pub and sign a petition or two.
S1.think: Privately I think I'm fine, because site carpentry is a hundred small decisions about wonky timber. A factory can cut panels, but someone still stands them up straight on a muddy plot.
S1.do: Waits until bigger firms have tested the new tools, then asks her boss for training on the ones that work. Uses the AI app more for planning the week and keeps saving at the same rate.
S1.feel: Calm and a little curious, with some concern for her cousin in the prefab factory.
S1.quote: We had a moisture-reading app that was wrong half the time. I'll pick it up once I've seen it work on someone else's job.
S1.fieldNote: Classic steady adopter: open but waiting for proof, with a concrete example of a failed gadget. Her concern goes to factory workers like her cousin rather than herself. Politics stays light: petitions and pub talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a disaster that governments let happen, and that the companies building it should be paying for everyone it puts out of work. I'd be at the protest outside parliament with Jonas, both of us. I'd post about it, which I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be terrified. I'm good, but if a robot can frame a house, then good doesn't matter. Jonas drives a bus, so if self-driving buses come with it, we're both out at the same time, and four months of savings doesn't stretch over two people for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop saving for a place and keep that money as a lifeboat. I'd cut the gym, the car would go and I'd cycle to site, and we'd look at moving in with my mum if it got bad. I'd join every action the union called, and I'd ring my MP's office, which I've never done in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like being on a roof when the wind picks up and there's nothing to hold. My chest goes tight just saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the first conversation with Jonas sound like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably we'd laugh first, because it's so big it's stupid, and then we'd sit up too late doing sums on the back of an envelope. He's calmer than me, he'd say "we've got your mum's spare room". I'd say I don't want to be twenty-nine and back in my old bedroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try to retrain in those two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to, but into what? If everything's going, I'd rather put my energy into getting a proper basic income passed. Maybe a short course in something like site safety, just so I'm the person who checks the robots.

S2.say: I'd say governments let a disaster happen and the companies building AGI should pay for everyone it puts out of work. I'd protest outside parliament with Jonas and post about it, which I never do.
S2.think: Honestly I'd be terrified: if a robot can frame a house, being good doesn't matter. Jonas drives a bus, so we could both be out at once, and four months of savings won't stretch over two people.
S2.do: Stops saving for a home and keeps the money as a lifeboat, cancels the gym and sells the car to cycle to site. Joins union actions, calls her MP for the first time and considers moving into her mum's spare room.
S2.feel: Terrified, with a tight chest, like being on a roof in rising wind with nothing to hold.
S2.quote: I'd say I don't want to be twenty-nine and back in my old bedroom.
S2.fieldNote: The double exposure through her partner's bus job drives her fear more than her own trade. She moves quickly from personal cutbacks to politics, which is new for her. Retraining feels pointless except for a narrow safety-checking role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them to write the rules before it lands. A public plan for retraining and a basic income, set up properly, not thrown together in a panic. I'd be pushing the union and the co-op to talk about it openly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years changes it for me. I'd have time to see which way it's going and move into something nearby, like being a building inspector or a site manager, where you're responsible for what goes up. Someone has to sign their name to the building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sign up for the site supervisor certificate at night school, it's about a year part-time. I'd keep saving but put the house deposit on hold until we see more. Around year three I'd start watching the first robot crews closely, and I'd try to get on a site that trials them so I learn how they work instead of being surprised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. Like having a deadline you can actually meet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is this different from the two-year picture for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Night and day. With two years I'd just be bailing water. With five, I can build a little boat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't the supervisor job at risk too, by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, probably, in the end. But I think the people who check and sign off will go last, because someone has to be blamed when it goes wrong. I'd rather be that person than the one who got replaced first.

S3.say: I'd say we've got five years, so let's write the rules now: a public retraining plan and a basic income set up properly, not in a panic. I'd push the union and the co-op to talk about it.
S3.think: Privately, five years lets me see where it's going and move into something nearby, like inspector or site manager. Someone has to sign their name to the building.
S3.do: Signs up for a one-year part-time site supervisor certificate in the first year and puts the house deposit on hold. Tries to get onto a site trialling robot crews around year three so she learns how they work.
S3.feel: Anxious but busy, like facing a deadline she can actually meet.
S3.quote: With two years I'd just be bailing water. With five, I can build a little boat.
S3.fieldNote: Five years flips her from bailing to planning. She knows the supervisor role is also exposed but bets accountability jobs go last. Very clear contrast drawn between timelines without prompting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this well if we start now. I'd want the government to fund apprenticeships into whatever new work comes, and the companies to pay into a fund. I'd probably get more involved in the union's education committee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be okay-ish. I'll be thirty-seven, so I'd have had time to move up, and maybe into teaching carpentry at the college. That's still a person in a room with young people, and I think that lasts a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the supervisor certificate in the next couple of years and then the teaching qualification. Jonas and I would probably still buy a small place, but with a short mortgage, fifteen years, so it's mostly paid when things change. I'd learn the AI tools properly too, once they're settled, because by 2030 I'd want to be the one who knows how to run them on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. It's a long road and I can see where I'm going on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your apprentices in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get your trade, but get a second string too, something with people in it. I'd tell them to go for the supervisor and teaching routes earlier than I did. And keep a bit of money aside, always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does a decade make you feel safer or does it just stretch the worry out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safer, mostly. The worry's still there, but it's like a cold you know you'll get over rather than a broken leg. I'd rather have ten years and a plan than two and a panic.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to do it well if we start now: government-funded apprenticeships into new work and companies paying into a fund. I'd get more involved in the union's education committee.
S4.think: Off the record I think I'd be okay-ish at thirty-seven, having moved up or into teaching carpentry at the college. A person in a room with young people lasts a while.
S4.do: Completes the supervisor certificate in the next two years, then a teaching qualification, and learns the AI tools properly once they settle. Buys a small place with Jonas on a short fifteen-year mortgage so it's mostly paid off by the change.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly fine, like a cold she knows she'll get over rather than a broken leg.
S4.quote: The worry's still there, but it's like a cold you know you'll get over rather than a broken leg.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade she builds a staged plan: supervision, then teaching, plus a short mortgage. Her steady nature shows in waiting for the tools to settle before learning them. Feels much safer than in the fast pictures.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Jonas and I could both lose our jobs at once. What would help is a real basic income that's ready to go, not something they argue about for three years while people lose their homes. And paid retraining you can actually live on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about women in the trades. It took us twenty years to get a few of us onto sites, and if the jobs vanish, the last ones in will be the first ones forgotten.

headlineQuote: If the jobs vanish, the last ones in will be the first ones forgotten.
portrait: Olga is a 27-year-old lead carpenter for a non-profit builder putting up timber-frame affordable homes, one of few women leading a crew. She uses an AI chat app now and then but checks everything against her own numbers, and waits for tools to prove themselves on someone else's job. In the mild pictures she is calm, protected by a long housing pipeline. Fast AGI terrifies her because her partner Jonas, a bus driver, could lose his job at the same moment; with five or ten years she builds a plan through supervising and then teaching. Her politics sharpen as the timeline shortens, from petitions to protests and calling her MP.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she and her partner Jonas could both lose their jobs at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income that is ready to go instead of argued over for years, and paid retraining people can actually live on.
